ai_summary:
The European Commission has proposed a regulation to set up "Global Europe," the EU's main external funding instrument, for the years 2028 to 2034. The aim is to promote the EU's values, principles and interests around the world, build mutually beneficial partnerships with non-EU countries, support their sustainable development, and help the Union respond to global challenges. The European Parliament will decide on the proposal through the ordinary legislative procedure, on an equal footing with the Council.

The proposal is part of the EU's next long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028 to 2034, which the Commission presented in July 2025 as a budget of EUR 2 trillion. The external part of that budget is meant to be simpler, more focused and more flexible, and to support a more strategic approach to enlargement, partnerships and diplomacy.

The instrument rests on four guiding principles. It would simplify the EU's external spending by bringing it under one main instrument and a shared performance rule for the whole budget. It would improve coherence by focusing more on specific regions, linking internal and external programmes, and strengthening a "Team Europe" approach. It would keep some of the flexibility of the current instrument, including its general reserve and the ability to move money between areas. And it would aim for greater impact by offering a broader set of tools, a streamlined framework for guarantees and blending funds, and stronger promotion of European interests.

The instrument would cover a range of goals, including expanding economic and trade opportunities, supporting sustainable development, promoting human rights and gender equality, and tackling the root causes of irregular migration, forced displacement, instability, climate change and environmental damage. It would also give candidate countries support to bring their laws, standards and practices closer to EU rules, through performance-based plans.

The total budget for the period from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2034 would be EUR 200.3 billion, divided among six areas: Europe (EUR 43.174 billion), the Middle East, North Africa and the Gulf (EUR 42.934 billion), Sub-Saharan Africa (EUR 60.531 billion), Asia and the Pacific (EUR 17.050 billion), the Americas and the Caribbean (EUR 9.144 billion), and global programmes (EUR 12.668 billion). In addition, up to EUR 100 billion in loans for Ukraine would be made available through the instrument.

Finally, the proposal aims to build a new European economic foreign policy and align external action more closely with EU domestic priorities, such as economic security, competitiveness, energy security, migration, climate, connectivity and access to critical raw materials.

This proposal would update the EU rules on key information documents (KIDs), the short plain-language documents that explain the features, risks and costs of packaged retail and insurance-based investment products (PRIIPs). These products are often offered by banks to ordinary savers, for example to save for a house or a child's education, but they can be complicated and hard to compare. The existing rules, set out in Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014, require producers and sellers to give investors these documents. The proposal keeps the main framework but makes targeted changes to it. The European Parliament and the Council would decide on it together, on an equal footing.

The main changes update the legal references to the prospectus rules, so the right securities are covered. They also remove retail products that provide immediate annuities with no redemption phase from the scope of the rules. For products that offer several investment options, the proposal sets out the conditions for presenting costs clearly, so investors can compare the choices.

The documents would also change in content. A new "Product at a glance" section would summarise the type of product, its costs, its level of risk, its recommended holding period and whether it includes an insurance benefit. The "comprehension alert," which warns about especially complex products, would be removed because it had not worked well and could discourage people from buying simpler products. A new section titled "How environmentally sustainable is this product?" would give investors a standard set of information on the sustainability of relevant products.

Finally, the proposal modernises how the documents are delivered. Electronic delivery would be preferred, but clients could request a paper copy free of charge. The European Supervisory Authorities would be asked to draft technical standards on how the information is presented, including features that make it accessible to visually impaired readers.

The European Parliament has adopted a set of changes to a proposed EU directive that would simplify the rules for the Infrastructure for Spatial Information in the Union, known as INSPIRE. The vote was 515 in favour, 108 against, with 35 abstentions. The changes were sent to the committee responsible for negotiations with the other EU institutions.

The proposal is part of a wider EU effort to simplify environmental rules and to support the GreenData4All initiative. It would remove some technical requirements for network services and data sharing from the INSPIRE Directive, relying instead on general EU data legislation.

Parliament broadly supports the goal of simplifying the rules and making them consistent with general data law. However, it is concerned that some of the Commission's approach could weaken protections that are specific to environmental geographic data.

Parliament's main amendments stress that good environmental data is essential for making, carrying out, monitoring and enforcing EU environmental laws. Member States would need to make sure that spatial datasets and services are provided using open, documented, vendor-neutral standards, including those of the International Organization for Standardization and the Open Geospatial Consortium, and that the technical choices made do not stop data from being found, accessed, used and reused across borders.

On the network of services, Member States would have to make relevant spatial datasets available and accessible under the EU open data directive, in a way that supports discovery, access and comparability across the EU. Public authorities would have to be able to link their datasets to relevant data-sharing services, and third parties whose datasets meet the required metadata and interoperability rules could request the same option.

On data sharing, Member States would have to ensure that public authorities can access and exchange the spatial data they need to carry out public tasks affecting the environment. Where necessary, countries would adopt or keep national measures to make this access effective.

The European Parliament has voted on a proposed temporary rule that would let online messaging and communication providers use certain technologies to scan personal and other data in order to detect and fight online child sexual abuse. The rule would temporarily set aside some privacy requirements from an existing EU directive on electronic communications, and it applies to services that are not based on phone numbers.

Parliament proposed changes to the Council's version of the rule. Its main change would exclude from the rule any communications that use, have used, or will use end-to-end encryption, meaning messages that only the people communicating can read.

In the first vote, a simple majority voted against the Council's position, with 314 in favour of rejecting it, 276 against, and 17 abstentions. A second vote on rejecting Parliament's amended position did not get a majority, with 276 in favour, 286 against, and 30 abstentions. Because neither side won a majority in that second vote, the second reading has ended.

This measure sets out the rules for how the European Union handles the leftover money and assets of the European Coal and Steel Community, which expired in July 2002. Under an existing protocol, those assets are used to fund research in the coal and steel sectors through the Research Fund for Coal and Steel. The measure would be adopted as a Council Decision, and the Council can only adopt it if the European Parliament has given its consent.

The European Commission would be responsible for managing the assets and for putting in place the measures needed to carry out the protocol. The aim is to keep an annual research allocation of up to EUR 120 million for each year from 2027 to 2033. The reason for this is that the income from the assets has been falling, and in 2024 and 2025 the calls for research were paid for entirely by selling assets. From August 2027, the old Community is expected to have no remaining debts or claims, which would allow it to be wound up and make it possible to sell part of the assets.

Any assets left over after that period would form a final allocation for 2034, set at their market value when transferred to the fund, taking market conditions into account. That money would then go toward coal and steel research in 2034 and later years. The annual funding would come from investment income and cash raised by selling some assets, and it would be treated as earmarked revenue in the EU budget.

The research money would be split through work programmes, with 27.2% going to coal-related research and 72.8% to steel-related research. The steel research would focus on cleaner, low-carbon production, stronger steel products, resource conservation, recycling, skills, working conditions and digital technology. The coal research would focus on managing a fair transition, including reusing old or closing coal mines and their infrastructure and the regions around them. The Commission would be allowed to change the 27.2% and 72.8% split through delegated acts if needed to make full use of the assets in 2034.
